content.overview: Portable powered tools add energy, speed, moving parts, electrical or pneumatic connections, and stored momentum to work that may already occur in tight cultivation spaces. Safe use therefore starts before activation. The operator must verify that the tool is suitable, intact, correctly guarded or controlled for its design, supplied by an appropriate energy source, and usable without exposing coworkers, crop infrastructure, water lines, or the operator to avoidable hazards.

vocabulary.definition: A physical protective feature intended to reduce access to a hazardous moving part, cutting zone, nip point, or ejected material path.
A switch, trigger, throttle, or other control used to start, stop, or regulate a powered tool.
An inspection, setup, isolation, PPE, clearance, or work-area action completed before a powered tool is energized.

sections.title: Verify safe condition and intended configuration
sections.body: Start with the manufacturer's intended configuration and the workplace tool procedure. OSHA requires tools and equipment to be maintained in safe condition, and specific portable-tool provisions require guarding and controls for covered tools. Check housing, handles, guards, switches, accessories, fasteners, cords or hoses, and signs of damage or unauthorized modification. A missing guard, cracked component, damaged cord, sticking control, or wrong accessory is a reason to stop and remove the tool from normal use until the condition is corrected through the authorized process.

sections.title: Control the work zone before energizing
sections.body: Identify where hands, coworkers, crop supports, irrigation tubing, electrical cords, benches, and finished surfaces will be when the tool starts. Secure or support the workpiece when needed; maintain clearance from the tool's operating path; and manage chips, dust, fragments, vibration, noise, heat, or kickback according to the specific tool and task. Do not rely on reaction time as the primary safeguard. The safer sequence is to make the hazardous path predictable before energy is applied.

sections.title: Plan energy connection and shutdown
sections.body: Portable electric tools and extension cords require pre-use visual inspection for external defects under OSHA's equipment-use rule. Pneumatic, battery, hydraulic, or other powered equipment has different energy and stored-energy concerns. The operator should know how the tool is stopped, how accidental activation is prevented during setup or accessory changes, and what condition requires disconnection or formal maintenance isolation. Course examples do not replace equipment-specific instructions or facility energy-control procedures.

workedExamples: A portable drill has a cracked cord jacket near the plug. The operator removes it from service rather than wrapping the damaged area and continuing the task.
A cutting tool is functional but its intended guard is missing. The operator does not accept careful hand placement as a substitute for restoring the tool to its required configuration.
commonMistakes: Checking whether a powered tool runs but not whether guards, controls, accessories, cords, or housings are safe.
Plugging in or installing a battery before the workpiece and operating zone are controlled.
Assuming an experienced operator can compensate for defective or modified equipment.
content.practicalApplication: Use a de-energized or simulated powered tool to conduct a pre-use briefing. Identify tool condition, guard/control checks, accessory fit, work-zone hazards, energy connection, shutdown method, and at least three stop-work conditions before simulated activation.
content.summary: Powered-tool safety begins with safe condition, correct configuration, a controlled operating zone, and a planned energy/shutdown sequence. Skill does not replace guards, inspections, or equipment-specific controls.
